newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: "Lebed factor" seen limited for Swiss franc.
newsitem.headline: "Lebed factor" seen limited for Swiss franc.

text.p: The Swiss franc has only limited room to rise against the mark on investor jitters sparked by Russian President Boris Yeltsin's sacking of his security chief Alexander Lebed, currency analysts said.

The Swiss National Bank's (SNB) expansive monetary policy that is keeping short-term money market rates around 1-1/2 percent should rob the franc of much upward momentum unless events in Moscow spin seriously out of control, they said.

"Mark/Swiss is certainly vulnerable to a further downward correction if events in Russia continue to deteriorate," CS Research said in its daily forex trading strategy bulletin, highlighting the franc's traditional safe haven role.

"On the other hand, some international players...seem to have misinterpreted the rise in (money) rates this week. So the return to levels of 1.5 percent for day-to-day money next week could boost mark/Swiss, especially if the dollar trades higher."
The mark lost around 30 basis points against the franc on Lebed's sacking to trade around 82.15 Swiss centimes Thursday. It was steady around 82.25 centimes today.
Zurich Cantonal Bank said the uncertainty surrounding Russia could keep weighing on the mark, but primarily measured against the dollar rather than against the franc.

"After news emerged that Yeltsin had sacked Lebed, one saw the mark post hefty losses against the dollar and the franc. The newly rekindled Russia problem is an additional factor that could drive the greenback higher," it said in a market outlook.
CS Research analyst Rainer Marian said Lebed was not much of a factor in the longer-term outlook for the franc.
"We saw a direct reaction, but we are getting back to normal," he said, adding Lebed would have a hard time forming an effective opposition because he was not backed by a party apparatus.

"The fact that Lebed is no longer in government may have a long-term impact, but not in the short term. From this aspect, this will not be a big factor that will move us in the next 14 days," he said. "This is more or less a non-event."
The mark/franc remains in a rough trading range between 80 and 83.5 centimes, Marian said.
"If we really go over 83 then the agressiveness with which the SNB puts liquidity into the market will ease up," he said.
"On the lower side, it is clear that the stronger the franc gets, the lower interest rates will go and the more expansive monetary policy will be. I think we are trapped here for the time being."
